activities.caption: pair each statement with its translation
activities.name: expLogMatch

config.prompt: Pair each statement with what it says:

pairs.right: the power I must raise 2 to, to get 32

config.why: The log is the exponent — the exponential's undo button, and its mirror image across the line y = x.

activities.caption: file each extension under the law that forces it
activities.name: expExtSort

config.prompt: File each extension under the requirement that forces it:

items.label: because aⁿ ÷ aⁿ must equal aⁿ⁻ⁿ
because aⁿ × a⁻ⁿ must equal a⁰ = 1

config.why: The extensions were chosen to preserve the index laws — not invented as tricks.

config.prompt: One of these claims about zero exponents is wrong — click it:
lines: a⁰ = 0, because multiplying zero times gives nothing.
config.correction: a⁰ = 1 — any other definition would break every index law at once.
config.why: The pattern makes the answer obvious: divide by 2 each step and the next value must be 1.

activities.anchor: how many heartbeats in a lifetime
activities.caption: call the lifetime heartbeat count
activities.name: expHeartEst

config.prompt: Estimate: 70 beats per minute × 60 × 24 × 365 × 80 years — roughly how many heartbeats in a lifetime?
config.why: About 3 × 10⁹ — estimation problems are standard-form arithmetic plus nerve, exactly how professional scientists sanity-check claims.
config.context: orders of magnitude: a rat is 10² times a mouse, a human 10² times a rat

activities.anchor: Decay is the same law running backwards
activities.caption: growth versus decay — drag the divider
activities.name: expLawCompare

config.prompt: The same law, two directions — drag the divider:

before.label: growth
before.text: A = A₀(1 + r)ⁿ — constant percentage means ever-larger absolute change, concave-up

after.label: decay
after.text: N = N₀(½)^(t/T) — halves whatever remains, never quite reaching zero

config.why: Decay keeps a schedule for halves, not for the last atom — the horizontal asymptote in action.

activities.anchor: a charcoal sample from a fire pit holds 25%
activities.caption: call the charcoal's age
activities.name: expCarbonEst

config.prompt: Charcoal holds 25% of the living carbon-14 ratio (half-life 5,730 years). Roughly how old is the sample?
config.why: 25% is two halvings, so 2 × 5,730 = 11,460 years — archaeology's clock is exponential decay plus a logarithm.

activities.anchor: Three laws follow immediately from the index laws
activities.caption: fill the blanks — the log laws
activities.name: expLawCloze

config.text: The log laws: log(ab) = log a %%0%% log b — multiplying becomes adding; log(a/b) = log a − log b — division becomes subtraction; and log(aⁿ) = %%1%%·log a — powers become coefficients.
config.hint: What sign the product law uses, and what factor the power law produces.

activities.caption: find the law that does not exist
activities.name: expSumSpot

config.prompt: One of these log laws is fake — click it:
lines: log(ab) = log a + log b — multiplying becomes adding.
log(a + b) = log a + log b.
config.correction: There is no law for log(a + b) — combine the addition first, then log.
config.why: Check with a = b = 1: log 2 ≈ 0.301 but log 1 + log 1 = 0.

config.root: Solve 3ˣ = 20. A student writes x = log 20 − log 3 ≈ 0.82. What went wrong?

choices.label: Nothing — the subtraction is the right move
choices.feedback: The power law says log(aⁿ) = n·log a — but here the unknown is the exponent: x = log 20 / log 3 ≈ 2.73, division not subtraction.

choices.label: The exponent comes out as a ratio of logs: x = log 20 / log 3 ≈ 2.73
choices.feedback: Right — take log of both sides, apply the power law, and divide.

choices.label: Try integer values first
choices.feedback: Guessing works for 3ˣ = 27 but not 20 — the log route is general.

wrong.text: Subtracting logs belongs to log(a/b), not to an unknown exponent.

right.text: n = log(goal/start) / log(1 + r) — one formula for every 'how long?' question growth can pose.

guess.text: The log route answers every case, integer or not.

config.why: Solving exponential equations is the payoff: log both sides, apply the power law, divide.

activities.caption: drop the marker — the earthquake ratio
activities.name: expQuakePlace

config.prompt: On the earthquake magnitude scale, each whole number is roughly how many times more energy released?
config.why: About 32-fold per whole number — a magnitude 7 is not 'a bit worse' than a 6, it is a different category of event.
